slides.heading: Dust of Snow — Robert Frost
slides.body_md:
*First Flight*, poetry · Class 10 CBSE English.

**Read the poem itself in your textbook, *First Flight* (NCERT), aloud, twice.** This lesson is SOYL's explanation; it does not reproduce the poem.

slides.narration: Welcome. Today’s poem is Dust of Snow by Robert Frost. It is one of the shortest poems in your book, just eight lines, so please read it in First Flight now, aloud, twice. We will not repeat its lines here. Instead we will understand what happens, why it matters, the symbols Frost chooses, and how to answer board questions on it.

slides.heading: How to read a short poem
bullets: Read it aloud twice from *First Flight*; notice where the sentence ends.
Ask: what happens? how does the speaker feel before and after?
Then ask: why these images, this bird, this tree?
In answers, explain in your own words; never copy lines.
slides.narration: Short poems reward slow reading. First, read it aloud twice and notice where the sentence ends. Then ask two simple questions: what happens, and how does the speaker feel before and after? Finally ask why Frost chose these particular images. When you answer in the exam, explain in your own words. Copying lines does not earn marks.

slides.heading: The poet: Robert Frost

rows: poems set in the farms and woods of New England, in plain everyday language with deeper meanings
Pulitzer Prize for Poetry, four times
*The Road Not Taken*, *Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening*, *Fire and Ice*

visual.alt: Table of facts about Robert Frost: American poet, 1874 to 1963, known for New England poems in plain language, four-time Pulitzer Prize winner, author of The Road Not Taken and Fire and Ice; Dust of Snow appears in New Hampshire, 1923.

slides.narration: Robert Frost was an American poet who lived from eighteen seventy-four to nineteen sixty-three. He wrote about farms, woods and ordinary country life in New England, in plain language that hides deep ideas. He won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry four times. You may know his poem The Road Not Taken, and Fire and Ice is also in your book.

slides.heading: The poem at a glance

rows: one sentence running through the whole poem
a person outdoors on a winter day, in a low mood
beneath a snow-covered hemlock, with a crow above
plain report → quiet gratitude and relief

visual.alt: Table of the poem at a glance: eight lines in two quatrains, a single sentence, rhyme scheme abab cdcd, a speaker in a low mood outdoors in winter, a hemlock and a crow, and a tone moving from plain report to gratitude.

slides.narration: Here is the poem at a glance. Eight short lines in two stanzas of four. Remarkably, the whole poem is one sentence. The rhyme scheme is a b a b, c d c d. The speaker is outdoors on a winter day, in a low mood, under a snowy hemlock with a crow above. The tone moves from a plain report to quiet gratitude.

slides.heading: Stanza 1: the incident
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: a crow perched in a snow-laden hemlock disturbs a branch, and a light sprinkle of snow falls on the speaker standing below. That is all that happens: a second-long event, reported plainly.
slides.narration: The first stanza records the incident. A crow sitting in a hemlock moves, and some fine snow from the branch falls on the speaker below. Nothing more happens. Notice how ordinary it is, and how plainly it is told. Frost gives a whole stanza to an event that lasts barely a second, as if to say that small moments deserve our attention.

slides.heading: Stanza 2: the effect
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: the speaker had been regretting the day. The cold touch of snow lifts his spirits, and he feels that the remainder of that unhappy day has been rescued. The change is quiet, not wild joy.
slides.narration: The second stanza gives the effect. The speaker had been having a day he regretted. The sudden cold touch of the snow jolts him out of that mood, and he feels that the rest of the day has been rescued. Notice that he does not claim great happiness. The change is real but quiet, which is typical of Frost.

slides.heading: Check: what changed the speaker's mood?
slides.narration: Your turn. Think about where the speaker’s better mood comes from. Is it something we would normally expect to cheer a person up? Choose the answer that captures the surprise.

slides.heading: The speaker's experience

nodes.label: A tiny event: snow falls from a branch

visual.alt: Flow of the speaker’s experience: a low mood, a tiny event as snow falls from a branch, a cold sudden touch, the mood lifts, and the rest of the day is rescued.
visual.caption: The speaker's experience (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: Here is the whole experience as a flow. A low, regretful mood. A tiny event, snow falling from a branch. A cold and sudden touch. The mood lifts. And the rest of the day is rescued. If you can explain these five steps in your own words, you can answer almost any question on the poem.

slides.heading: Symbols: the crow and the hemlock
slides.body_md: Frost could have chosen a songbird and a flowering tree. He chose two things readers link with gloom, and let them bring cheer.

headers: What it does in the poem
rows: causes the snow to fall: brings cheer
name of a poisonous plant (Socrates): sorrow, death
holds the snow that refreshes the speaker
a light, cool touch that wakes him up

visual.alt: Table of symbols: the crow usually means ill omen but brings cheer; the hemlock suggests sorrow and death but holds the refreshing snow; snow suggests bleak winter but gives a cool, waking touch.
visual.caption: The poem reverses the usual meanings.

slides.narration: Why a crow and a hemlock? In folklore the crow, black and harsh voiced, is often an ill omen. The hemlock shares its name with a poisonous plant, the one linked with the death of Socrates, so it suggests sorrow and death. Snow suggests bleak winter. Yet together they lift the speaker’s mood. Frost reverses their usual meanings.

slides.heading: Expectation versus outcome
columns:
**What we expect**

- a crow: bad luck
- a hemlock: poison, death
- snow: cold, bleakness
- a bad day: stays bad

**What happens**

- the crow causes a helpful surprise
- the hemlock holds the refreshing snow
- the snow wakes the speaker up
- the rest of the day is rescued
slides.narration: Set expectation beside outcome and the irony is clear. We expect the crow to bring bad luck, the hemlock to suggest death, the snow to feel bleak, and a bad day to stay bad. Instead, each of them helps. This contrast carries the message: comfort can come from unlikely places, so we should not judge things only by their usual meanings.

slides.heading: Check: symbols and their meaning
slides.narration: Check yourself with an assertion and reason. Both statements may be true, but does the second really explain the first? Think about what actually lifts the speaker’s mood.

slides.heading: Themes and message
bullets: **Small moments matter:** a second-long event changes a day.
**Nature as healer:** no person comforts the speaker; nature does.
**Hope from unlikely sources:** gloomy symbols bring cheer.
**Moods can change:** one bad morning need not spoil the whole day.
slides.narration: The themes follow naturally. Small moments matter, since a second long event changes a day. Nature heals, because no person comforts the speaker; nature does. Hope can come from unlikely sources, even gloomy ones. And moods are not fixed: one bad morning need not spoil the whole day. In answers, state a theme and support it with the incident.

slides.heading: Poetic devices, with SOYL's own examples
slides.body_md: Each device is described in the poem and illustrated with a SOYL sentence, not with the poem's lines.

headers: A SOYL example of the device

The *owl* on the gate stood for every fear of the night.
sight of the dark bird and white snow; touch of cold

visual.alt: Table of poetic devices in the poem, described, each with a SOYL example: symbolism, imagery, enjambment, rhyme scheme abab cdcd, and irony or contrast.

slides.narration: Now the devices. Symbolism, in the crow and hemlock. Imagery of sight and touch: the dark bird, the white powder, the cold. Enjambment, as one sentence runs across all eight lines. A rhyme scheme of a b a b, c d c d. And irony, as gloomy symbols bring cheer. The examples in the right column are our own sentences, made to show each device.

slides.heading: Why enjambment suits this poem
slides.body_md: The poem's single sentence never pauses until the end. Read it aloud from *First Flight* and notice that you hardly stop for breath.
bullets: **Form:** one unbroken sentence across eight short lines.
**Experience:** the snow falls and the mood changes almost at once.
**Link:** the quick, unbroken movement of the sentence mirrors the swift change.
slides.narration: Here is a worked point you can use in answers. The poem is a single sentence that runs on from line to line. Read aloud, it barely pauses. That quick, unbroken movement mirrors the experience: the snow falls and, almost at once, the mood changes. When form and meaning match like this, say so in your answer. It shows real understanding.

slides.heading: Tone and mood
slides.body_md: Stanza 1 is plain and descriptive. Stanza 2 is reflective, grateful and relieved. Frost never names the cause of the bad mood, so every reader can supply their own bad day.
slides.narration: Listen to the tone. The first stanza is plain, almost like a report. The second is reflective and grateful. Notice too what Frost leaves out: he never tells us why the speaker was unhappy. That silence is clever. It lets every reader imagine their own bad day, a failed test or a quarrel, and so the poem feels personal to everyone.

slides.heading: Word meanings

rows: a large black bird; in folklore, often an ill omen
an evergreen conifer of North America; also the name of a poisonous plant
a state of mind or feeling

visual.alt: Table of word meanings: crow, hemlock, dust, rued and mood.
visual.caption: Single words from the poem with their meanings.

slides.narration: A few words to know. Crow, a large black bird often seen as an ill omen. Hemlock, an evergreen tree whose name is shared with a poisonous plant. Dust, here meaning fine powdery snow. Rued, meaning regretted. And mood, a state of mind. Rued is the word students most often get wrong, so learn it well.

slides.heading: Check: the rhyme scheme
slides.narration: Quick check. Write the rhyme scheme of the poem using letters. Look at which lines in each stanza end with matching sounds, in your textbook.

slides.heading: Worked example: a 40–50 word answer
slides.body_md: *Question:* How does a small incident lift the speaker's spirits?
bullets: **Point:** a tiny natural event ends his gloom.
**Incident (own words):** a crow in a hemlock shakes snow onto him while he is regretting his day.
**Support:** the cold touch jolts him; the rest of the day feels rescued.

**Model (46 words):** *The speaker is in a gloomy mood, regretting how his day has gone. A crow in a hemlock shakes some snow onto him. The sudden, cold touch of nature jolts him out of his sadness, and he feels that the rest of the day has been rescued.*

nodes.label: Device or symbol that supports it

visual.alt: Flow for a forty to fifty word answer: find the key word, state the point, give the incident in your own words, add a supporting device or symbol.

slides.narration: Here is how to build a three mark answer. Find the key word: lift. State the point: a tiny natural event ends his gloom. Describe the incident in your own words. Add support: the cold touch jolts him, and the day feels rescued. The model answer is forty-six words, inside the limit, and it does not copy a single line of the poem.

slides.heading: Check: the word rued
slides.narration: One more. What does the word rued mean? It tells you how the speaker felt about his day before the snow fell.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Incident: a crow in a hemlock shakes snow onto the speaker.
Effect: his regretful mood lifts; the rest of the day is rescued.
Symbols reversed: crow and hemlock (gloom) bring cheer.
Form: 8 lines, 2 quatrains, one sentence, abab cdcd, enjambment.
Message: small moments of nature can change our outlook. Read the poem in *First Flight*.

visual.caption: The speaker's experience (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: Let us sum up. A crow in a hemlock shakes snow onto the speaker. His regretful mood lifts, and the rest of his day is rescued. The crow and hemlock, usually symbols of gloom, bring cheer. The poem is eight lines, two quatrains, one sentence, rhyming a b a b, c d c d. Its message: small moments of nature can change our outlook.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Never write out the poem's lines; explain the idea in your own words.
Name devices **and** say what they do: *the crow is a symbol of ill omen, but here it brings cheer*.
For the hemlock, mention the association with poison and death (Socrates).
40–50 word answers: point + incident + device or symbol.
Common slips: saying the crow attacks the speaker; *rued* as "ruined"; calling the rhyme scheme aabb.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Never write out the lines; explain in your own words. When you name a device, also say what it does. For the hemlock, mention its link with poison and death. Keep three mark answers to point, incident and device. And avoid the common slips: the crow does not attack anyone, rued means regretted, not ruined, and the rhyme scheme is a b a b.

notes.title: Dust of Snow — study notes

sections.heading: 1. The poet and the poem
sections.body_md:
**Read the poem itself in your textbook, *First Flight* (NCERT), aloud, twice.** This lesson is SOYL's explanation; it does not reproduce the poem.

**Robert Frost** (1874–1963) was an American poet who wrote about country life in New England in plain, everyday language with deeper meanings. He won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry four times. *Dust of Snow* is a short lyric collected in *New Hampshire* (1923).

rows: poems set in the farms and woods of New England, in plain everyday language with deeper meanings
Pulitzer Prize for Poetry, four times
*The Road Not Taken*, *Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening*, *Fire and Ice*

visual.alt: Table of facts about Robert Frost: American poet, 1874 to 1963, known for New England poems in plain language, four-time Pulitzer Prize winner, author of The Road Not Taken and Fire and Ice; Dust of Snow appears in New Hampshire, 1923.

sections.heading: 2. What happens (SOYL summary)
sections.body_md:
**Stanza 1 — the incident:** on a winter day, a crow perched in a snow-covered hemlock disturbs a branch, and a light sprinkle of snow falls on the speaker below.

**Stanza 2 — the effect:** the speaker had been regretting how the day had gone. The sudden cold touch lifts his spirits, and he feels that the rest of that unhappy day has been rescued.

The poem is told in the first person, looking back on a moment and its effect.

nodes.label: A tiny event: snow falls from a branch

visual.caption: The speaker's experience (SOYL summary).

sections.heading: 3. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **Small moments matter:** a second-long incident changes the course of a day.
- **Nature as healer:** the speaker is helped by nature, not by people.
- **Hope from unlikely sources:** symbols of gloom bring cheer.
- **Moods can change:** a bad beginning need not mean a bad day.

Because the cause of the bad mood is never named, every reader can apply the poem to their own life.

sections.heading: 4. Symbols, imagery and devices
sections.body_md:
**Crow:** traditionally an ill omen (black, harsh-voiced). **Hemlock:** the North American tree is a harmless evergreen conifer, but it shares its name with a poisonous plant used to put Socrates to death, so readers take it as a symbol of sorrow or death. **Snow:** usually bleak winter; here a light, refreshing touch. The poem reverses all three.

**Devices:** symbolism; imagery of sight (dark bird, white powder) and touch (cold); enjambment (one sentence across eight lines); rhyme scheme abab cdcd; irony / contrast (gloomy symbols, cheerful effect).

**Form:** eight short lines, two quatrains, a single sentence; plain words.

sections.heading: 7. Answering exam questions
sections.body_md:
**Extract-based (5 marks):** the board prints the poem's lines; SOYL practice uses commentary passages instead. Expect questions on meaning, tone, devices and the rhyme scheme.

**Short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words):** point + incident in your own words + a device or symbol.

Practise with the poem itself in *First Flight*; never reproduce its lines in an answer.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** reference-to-context extract (5) and short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words) on First Flight poems (CBSE 2026-27, Section C).

**How marks are awarded:** a correct point, support from the poem in your own words, and accurate expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Writing out the poem instead of explaining it.
2. Saying the crow attacks the speaker or that he falls ill from the cold.
3. Reading *rued* as *ruined*.
4. Giving the rhyme scheme as aabb.
5. Naming a device without saying what it does in the poem.

**Remember:** read the poem in your textbook, *First Flight*.

questions.passage_md: The first half of Frost's poem records an incident that lasts barely a second. A crow, perched in a hemlock, disturbs a branch, and a light shower of snow falls on the speaker standing below. Nothing dramatic happens; no words are spoken. Yet Frost gives this tiny moment a whole stanza, as if to say that the smallest events deserve our attention. The details are chosen with care: a bird and a tree that readers often link with gloom, and snow that touches the speaker gently rather than burying him. The stage is set for a surprise.

questions.passage_md: Frost could have chosen a robin and a rose bush. Instead he chose a crow and a hemlock. In much folklore the crow, black and harsh-voiced, is a bad omen. The hemlock shares its name with a poisonous plant, the one associated with the death of the Greek philosopher Socrates, so readers often take it as a sign of sorrow or death, even though the tree Frost knew is a harmless evergreen of North America. By letting these gloomy symbols bring cheer, Frost overturns our expectations. Comfort, he suggests, can come from the most unlikely sources.

questions.passage_md: For all its simplicity, the poem is carefully built. Its eight short lines fall into two stanzas of four, and the alternate lines of each stanza rhyme. More surprising, the whole poem is a single sentence: the thought runs on from line to line without a full stop until the very end. This running-on, called enjambment, mirrors the experience itself. The snow falls, and before we can pause, the speaker's mood has already lifted. Form and meaning move together, quickly and lightly, like the snow.

answer.model_answer_md: Dust of Snow describes an incident that lasts only a second. A crow sitting in a hemlock shakes a light shower of snow onto the speaker, who has been in a gloomy, regretful mood. This tiny event jolts him out of his sadness and rescues the rest of his day. The hemlock recalls a poisonous plant of the same name, the one linked with the death of Socrates, so it suggests sorrow and death. Snow, too, belongs to cold, bleak winter. Yet in this poem these very things bring cheer. When the crow shakes snow from the hemlock onto the speaker, his low mood lifts. Tuesday, late evening

This morning began badly. Everything seemed to go wrong, and by noon I was sure the day was wasted. I went out for a walk, lost in gloomy thoughts, and stopped beneath a snowy hemlock at the edge of the field. A crow, settling on a branch above me, sent a shower of powdery snow onto my head and shoulders. It was so sudden and so cold that I laughed out loud. Strangely, the dark bird and the dark tree had cheered me up. I walked home lighter, and the afternoon went far better than the morning. Perhaps a day is never entirely lost.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the North American hemlock that Frost knew is itself the poisonous plant that killed Socrates.
questions.solution_md: **False.** They share a name only: the tree is a harmless evergreen conifer; the poison came from a different plant called hemlock. Readers still treat the name as a symbol of death.
